article_content: Three state troopers have testified in the murder trial of former New England Patriots tight end Aaron Hernandez regarding evidence they recovered. The former NFL star is charged in the June 2013 death of Odin Lloyd, who was dating the sister of Hernandez’s fiancée. Trooper Zachary Johnson testified on Thursday about visiting Lloyd’s home in Massachusetts on the evening his body was discovered and informing his family of his death. He also described a safe found in the closet of Hernandez’s master bedroom in North Attleboro, which contained a digital scale and a dish with what appeared to be marijuana residue. Another trooper provided detailed testimony about retrieving video surveillance footage from Hernandez’s home. Hernandez’s defense team has challenged the state’s handling of evidence. On Wednesday, jurors heard from Azia Jenkins, uncle of Hernandez’s fiancée Shayanna Jenkins, who testified that Hernandez calmly stated, 'My endorsements are gone,' the day after Lloyd’s murder. Jenkins said Hernandez made the comment during a game of pool while watching Game 6 of the NBA Finals and appeared 'cool, calm, collected.' At the time of the killing, Hernandez held a $40 million contract with the Patriots and endorsement deals with CytoSport and Puma. He was arrested on June 26 and subsequently released by the Patriots. Enterprise employee Keelia Smyth testified that Hernandez returned a damaged Nissan Altima on June 17, 2013, and that she found a bullet lodged in chewed blue gum inside the car. She recalled Hernandez offering her the gum before leaving. Also on Wednesday, Superior Court Judge Susan Garsh ruled that prosecutors could not call Hernandez’s high school friend Robert Paradis to testify. Paradis had previously told the court — outside the jury’s presence — that Hernandez claimed to keep a .45-caliber firearm under the seat of his car and later asked Paradis to check if he’d left it behind. The judge deemed Paradis’s testimony inconsistent and potentially prejudicial.

article_content: Tickets to the 2014 Chelsea Flower Show have sold out faster than ever before — second only to last year’s centenary event — with all 161,000 tickets gone within hours. The surge in demand is largely attributed to the return of beloved TV gardener Alan Titchmarsh, who is unveiling his first show garden since 1985. Titchmarsh’s garden, titled 'From the Moors to the Sea', celebrates both his five decades as a professional gardener and the 50th anniversary of Britain in Bloom, a nationwide gardening initiative run by the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS). The design reflects his personal journey from the moorlands of Yorkshire to his holiday home on the Isle of Wight, featuring a dry-stone wall, heather, birch and pine trees, and a coastal section with sea kale and a beach hut. While official tickets range from £23 for evening entry to £68 for full-day access, secondary platforms like Seatwave and Viagogo are reselling them for up to £575 — including hefty booking fees. The RHS strongly advises against purchasing from unofficial sellers, warning that fake tickets will result in denied entry. To combat ticket scalping, the RHS is offering exclusive £400 charity tickets. Proceeds directly fund horticultural apprenticeships and grant holders early access to the show after public hours. 'This isn't just about tickets — it's about investing in the future of gardening,' said RHS spokeswoman Hayley Monckton. Titchmarsh, who has presented BBC’s Chelsea coverage for over 30 years, is not competing for awards this year — his garden is a commissioned piece as RHS Vice President. Still, he insists on delivering something extraordinary: 'I want people to say, 'Oh my goodness, look at that.' Other standout gardens include 'No Man’s Land' by Charlotte Rowe for ABF The Soldiers’ Charity and 'Hope on the Horizon' by Matthew Keightley for Help for Heroes — both honoring the centenary of World War I. Designers such as Cleve West, Hugo Bugg, and Sarah Eberle (for Gucci) are also presenting innovative displays, while 23-year-old David Rich becomes the youngest ever professional show garden designer. Queen Elizabeth II is expected to make her 50th appearance at the event, continuing her long-standing support for horticulture.

article_content: The group stage of the 2014 World Cup is now behind us — a perfect moment to pause and appreciate the drama, upsets, and brilliance we’ve witnessed. Out of the original 32 teams, 16 are heading home, including giants like reigning champions Spain, Cristiano Ronaldo’s Portugal, and England, whose campaigns ended far earlier than expected. But football loves surprises: tiny Costa Rica topped a group with Italy, England, and Uruguay; Greece scraped through with just two goals scored; and Algeria made history by advancing for the first time ever, beating Fabio Capello’s Russia. Now, as the knockout rounds begin, who truly shone brightest? With data from Opta, here are the 11 players who stood tallest in the first 48 matches. Vincent Enyeama, Nigeria’s goalkeeper, was impenetrable — two clean sheets to start, and it took a Messi masterpiece to beat him. He made 18 saves, the most in the tournament. Gary Medel, Chile’s compact defensive leader, was a wall against Spain, delivering 28 clearances and completing 93% of his 207 passes. Daniel van Buyten anchored Belgium’s tight wins, blocking five shots — more than anyone else. Rafael Márquez, captaining Mexico for the fourth World Cup, held firm, conceding just one goal and keeping Brazil’s Neymar quiet. Per Mertesacker, once overlooked, became Germany’s steady backbone, attempting 202 passes — second only to Medel among defenders. James Rodríguez stole the spotlight for Colombia: three goals, relentless creativity, and a goal or assist every 45 minutes — the best rate in the tournament. His teammate Juan Cuadrado, unleashed on the wing, delivered three assists, tying for the most. Arjen Robben lit up the tournament with three goals and an assist, including a dazzling run against Spain. Karim Benzema carried France’s attack, scoring three times and creating 12 scoring chances — tied for the most. Lionel Messi, ever the magician, scored four sublime goals, three from outside the box — more than any other player. And Neymar, carrying Brazil’s hopes, responded with four goals and a jaw-dropping 44.44% shot conversion rate. Honorable mentions: Ecuador’s Alexander Domínguez saved 85% of shots faced; Russia’s Ignashevich cleared 30 headers; Switzerland’s Shaqiri scored the first-ever left-footed World Cup hat-trick; and Germany’s Thomas Müller reached nine World Cup goals in nine appearances — matching Pele.

article_content: Hours after a Sudanese court sentenced Meriam Yehya Ibrahim — an eight-months-pregnant woman raised as a Christian — to death for refusing to renounce her faith, her husband, Daniel Wani, described feeling utterly powerless. 'I’m so frustrated. I don’t know what to do,' Wani told CNN. 'I’m just praying.' The Khartoum court convicted Ibrahim of apostasy and adultery, sentencing her to 100 lashes because, under Sharia law, her marriage to a Christian man is deemed invalid. Though Ibrahim identifies as Christian and was raised by her Ethiopian Orthodox mother after her Muslim father abandoned the family when she was six, the court classified her as Muslim based solely on paternal lineage. Despite being given a final chance to recant, she stood firm: 'I am a Christian, and I will remain a Christian,' she declared in court. Her lawyer, Mohamed Jar Elnabi, confirmed the verdict has drawn global outrage, with groups like Amnesty International calling her a prisoner of conscience. Ibrahim remains incarcerated alongside her 20-month-old son, who suffers from poor sanitation and frequent illness. Wani, who relies entirely on his wife for daily care, was barred from attending the hearing. Requests to move Ibrahim to a private hospital were denied over 'security concerns.' International embassies, including those of the U.S., UK, Canada, and Netherlands, have urged Sudan to uphold its constitutional and international obligations protecting freedom of religion. Human rights advocates argue that punishing apostasy or marital choices with death or flogging violates fundamental human rights standards. Meanwhile, Elnabi revealed he received a death threat days before the trial but vowed to continue defending Ibrahim: 'This is a matter of belief. I must help her, even if it costs me my life.' Sudan, long labeled one of the world’s worst violators of religious freedom, continues to enforce Sharia broadly, targeting Christians with imprisonment, church demolitions, and public lashings.

'Nagaa danda’u, maal akka danda’u hin fikirin,' Wani kanaa CNN irraa jedhe. 'Nagaa sirnaan.' Garaa Khartoumni Meriam yoo faallaa deebi’uuf hin qabne, faallaa fi fagaatee 100 jiraachuu danda’a jedhe, sababiin isaas maqaa Kristianii keessatti waliin walqabatee jiru kan shari’aan dhaabbatanii jiru. Akkasumas, Meriam Kristianii ta’uu danda’a, ishee gubbaa guddaa ta’e, oomii ittiyaa Ethioopiyaan Orthodoxii keessa qaba, kan babaasuu Muslimii ta’e ishee 6 olaanaa irratti gurgurte, garaa ishee oomii irraa dhaabbatanii jiru, garaa ishee babaasuu irraa deebi’uun Muslimii ta’uu danda’a. Meriam ishee 20 maqaan tokko ta’e namaa ishee keessatti gargaaru, isheen sirnaa hin qabne fi ga’umsa guddaa qaba. Wani, kan ishee keessatti duraan barbaachisa, dhaabbataa keessatti hundee dhaabbataa irraa hin jirre. Qabxii ishee gara haala sanaa qabsee qabsoo harka sanaa qabanii hin qabne. Dhaabbataa intanashinaalaa, U.S., UK, Canada, fi Netherlands, Sudan irraa dhaabbataa sirnaa deebi’uu fi maqaa deebi’uu dhaabbatu qabsoo dhaabbatanii jedhu. Barbaachisaa dhaabbataa ishee faallaa fi walqabatuu dhaabbatanii dhaabbataa intanashinaalaa sirnaa ture. Elnabi yeroo dhaabbataa kanaa karaa dhaabbataa argate jedhe, fi isheen Meriam dhaabbataa dhabamsiisuun danda’u jedhe: 'Kan dhaabbataa sirnaa jira. Ishee dhabamsiisuun danda’u, kan namni jiraachuu danda’u yoo ta’e.' Sudan, kan dhaabbataa sirnaa deebi’uu kanaa dunyaan garaa garaa guddaa ta’e, shari’aan guddaa dhaabbataa, Kristianootaaf garaa garaa dhaabbataa, dhaabbataa, fi qabsoo harka sanaa qabanii dhaabbataa.

article_content: Before their Europa League qualifier on Thursday night, fans of Aberdeen and FC Groningen were involved in violent clashes on the streets of the Netherlands. Multiple videos posted online showed supporters lining up on opposite sides of the road as police struggled to contain the unrest. Smoke bombs were detonated, causing panic among police horses. Despite the turmoil, Aberdeen secured a dramatic 2-1 away victory, advancing to the third qualifying round where they will face Real Sociedad. Aberdeen entered the match knowing an away goal could prove decisive after a goalless draw at Pittodrie. They took the lead in the 26th minute of the second leg when Ryan Rooney converted a penalty. Seven minutes later, Stuart McGinn capitalized on a rebound after Rooney hit the crossbar, doubling the lead. FC Groningen pulled one back just before halftime through Maikel Kieftenbeld, forcing Aberdeen to withstand intense pressure in the second half. However, a resilient defense — bolstered by Andrew Considine, who replaced Barry Robson — held firm, securing the win and delighting the visiting supporters.

Garaa garaa dhaabbatootni fankii jijjiramuu qabuun garaa garaa qaraxxaan yoo ta’een, barbaachisaa qabu. Fankii duraa duraa hawaasa qofaaf deebi’e. Kunis fankii kudhaa haaraa dhufuuf danda’ama. article_content: On New Year’s Day 2014, Julie De La Haut, 24, and her boyfriend Patrick Ochila, 31, were both convicted of drink-driving after being caught within hours of each other. The couple, who live together in Carterton, Oxfordshire, had been celebrating the new year when they got behind the wheel of their Nissan X-Trail after drinking. Shortly before 4 a.m., Ochila was pulled over by police after being reported for suspicious driving. A roadside breath test revealed he had 67 micrograms of alcohol per 100 millilitres of breath — nearly double the legal limit of 35. He was taken to Oxford Police Station, leaving De La Haut alone, intoxicated, and stranded in a dark car park with no cash for a taxi. At 5:10 a.m., officers spotted the Nissan moving through the car park near the Oxpens Road ice rink — without its headlights on. De La Haut was stopped moments later and registered an even higher breath alcohol level: 81 micrograms per 100 millilitres. Both appeared in Oxford Magistrates Court minutes apart to plead guilty. Their defence highlighted their remorse, lack of prior convictions, and the hardship of losing their ability to drive — especially since Ochila works for BT and they rely on the car for daily responsibilities. Presiding magistrate Roger Clarke called Ochila a 'decent, honest, hard-working family man' and expressed disappointment but hope that his employer would support him. De La Haut was acknowledged as having been in a 'difficult and vulnerable position', though the court stressed that driving without lights and while intoxicated remained serious offences. Ochila received an 18-month driving ban, a £375 fine, £85 in costs, and a £37 victim surcharge. De La Haut was banned for 20 months, fined £300, and charged a £30 surcharge. The judge urged both to learn from the incident and move forward.

article_content: Arkadi Gontmakher, an American entrepreneur once known as the 'King Crab King,' is fighting not just for his freedom — but for his life. After being cleared of all charges by a Russian jury in 2010, he was arrested again within minutes, accused of nearly the same crimes he’d already been found innocent of. Now 53 and confined to a hospital in remote Kamchatka under police watch, Gontmakher suffers from life-threatening heart arrhythmias and chronic kidney failure. His heart rate regularly spikes above 170 beats per minute, and he experiences daily episodes lasting up to 14 hours. Despite urgent medical needs, Russia refuses to allow him the specialized cardiac surgery he requires. Gontmakher insists he never fished for crabs himself; he simply bought pre-processed crab from licensed Russian suppliers who shipped the product through South Korea with full documentation. He ran a legitimate import business — Global Fishing Inc. — based in Washington state, which collapsed after his 2007 arrest. Russian investigators claim new evidence justifies the renewed charges, but Gontmakher’s lawyer argues this is a pattern of harassment designed to crush a successful foreign competitor. His wife says their younger son, now eight, hasn’t seen his father in over three years. With no end in sight, the family fears the Russian justice system is using the law as a weapon — not to uphold it.

article_content: For generations, Britons have turned to everything from greasy breakfasts to painkillers in search of a miracle cure for hangovers. But now, the NHS — the country’s publicly funded health service — has cut through the noise with straightforward advice: the best way to avoid a hangover is to not drink too much in the first place. On its NHS Choices website, officials have published a practical guide debunking long-held myths, from the infamous 'hair of the dog' to the classic bacon sandwich. While these remedies might feel comforting, they don’t actually fix anything. Instead, the NHS recommends simple, science-informed steps: eat a meal rich in carbs like pasta or rice before heading out, sip water or non-carbonated drinks between alcoholic ones, and finish the night with a full glass of water. If you’re feeling rough the next morning, the guide gently notes, you likely skipped these tips. For relief, paracetamol is safer than aspirin, which can worsen nausea. Surprisingly, the top-recommended remedy isn’t a meal but a warm bowl of bouillon soup — a light broth packed with electrolytes and easy on an upset stomach. The NHS warns that drinking more alcohol to 'cure' a hangover only delays discomfort and increases health risks. They also advise waiting at least 48 hours before drinking again. Adding to the conversation, migraine expert Dr. Andy Dowson suggests milk as a nighttime ally. Unlike water, milk helps restore blood sugar, reduces urine production (so you sleep better), and may soothe stomach irritation thanks to its alkaline nature. In short: skip the hangover cure myths. Stay hydrated, eat smart, rest well — and maybe, just maybe, lay off the booze altogether.

article_content: Michael Sheen and Ruth Wilson star in 'A Very Royal Scandal', a three-part Prime Video limited series dramatizing the explosive 2019 Newsnight interview where Prince Andrew defended his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein — a moment that led to his withdrawal from royal duties. The series centers on journalist Emily Maitlis (played by Wilson) as she navigates the intense pressure of holding power to account, while Sheen portrays Prince Andrew’s increasingly strained attempts to justify his actions. Supporting roles include Joanna Scanlan as Amanda Thirsk, Alex Jennings as Sir Edward Young, and Éanna Hardwicke as Stewart Maclean. Directed by Julian Jarrold and written by Jeremy Brock, the production is helmed by Blueprint Television for Amazon MGM Studios and distributed worldwide by Sony Pictures Television. Prince Andrew’s now-infamous claims — that he was dining at a Pizza Express on the night he allegedly met Virginia Giuffre, and that a rare medical condition prevented him from sweating — were widely ridiculed and became emblematic of his disconnect from public sentiment. Sheen, known for 'Good Omens', and Wilson, acclaimed for 'The Affair' and 'The Woman in the Wall', deliver compelling performances in this gripping retelling of a defining moment in modern British history.

Photos show Pacquiao smiling for selfies and cheering from the sidelines during the game.

QPR manager Harry Redknapp has already made five summer signings, the most recent being Juventus defender Mauricio Isla, who joined earlier this week.

article_content: Key documents concerning the murder of Alexander Litvinenko must remain secret, a UK court ruled yesterday. The coroner investigating the 2006 poisoning of the former KGB officer in London had planned to release a government dossier on the case. However, three judges at the High Court overruled him, stating that public disclosure would cause 'significant damage to national security.' This decision is another setback for Litvinenko’s family, who have long sought the truth behind his death. His widow, Marina, fears the alleged involvement of the Russian state may never be fully exposed. She plans to pursue legal action to compel the government to hold a full public inquiry—an option officials rejected earlier this year. Litvinenko was poisoned in November 2006 with polonium-210 after meeting two former KGB agents, Andrei Lugovoy and Dmitry Kovtun, at the Millennium Hotel in Mayfair. He died three weeks later. Both men deny involvement, and Russia has refused to extradite them for questioning in the UK. Coroner Sir Robert Owen argued that some classified material should be made public to ensure a 'fair and meaningful inquest.' But government lawyers insisted the documents were 'sensitive to the highest degree.' Lord Justice Goldring and two other judges agreed, concluding that the coroner had underestimated the national security risks—a legal error. Goldring emphasized that their ruling did not diminish the principle of open justice. Through her lawyer, Ben Emmerson QC, Marina Litvinenko said she was 'disappointed but not surprised.' She intends to appeal the government’s refusal to hold a public inquiry, calling it her final effort to reveal the Russian state’s responsibility in her husband’s death. The coroner excluded extensive classified material—including evidence related to Russian actors and whether British intelligence could have prevented his death. The scope of included evidence remains undisclosed. Last year, the inquest heard that Litvinenko had been working for MI6 and Spain’s secret service after fleeing Russia following disputes with his superiors and two arrests.

article_content: Maria Hinojosa, an acclaimed journalist and author, joined NOW on PBS as a senior correspondent in 2005. Previously covering urban affairs for CNN, she is also the anchor and managing editor of NPR’s 'Latino USA,' a nationally syndicated program highlighting Latino news and culture. In a deeply personal reflection, Hinojosa recounts asking her 11-year-old daughter, Yurema, which T-shirt she’d choose: 'I am a Wise Latina,' 'My Mother is a Wise Latina,' or 'Sonia is a Wise Latina.' Without hesitation, Yurema replied, 'I am a Wise Latina.' For Hinojosa, this moment captured the quiet triumph of a girl claiming her own power — a vision she once doubted possible for Latinas. Hinojosa admits that, like many Latinas, she has long carried deep-seated insecurities about her place alongside white male colleagues. Witnessing Sotomayor’s historic nomination in 2009, however, shattered those doubts. 'I can’t go back to thinking that way, anymore, ever,' she writes. Where once saying 'I am a Latina' invited stereotypical assumptions, now it might evoke the image of a 'wise Latina' — a phrase reclaimed from a controversial 2001 Supreme Court remarks by Justice Sotomayor and transformed into a badge of pride. Hinojosa contrasts her childhood — where the only Puerto Rican woman she knew was Natalie Wood’s Maria from 'West Side Story' — with her daughter’s reality: Sonia Sotomayor embodies intelligence, compassion, and linguistic mastery that transcend ethnic and political borders. When Yurema learns Senator John McCain plans to vote against Sotomayor’s confirmation, she calls him 'a big jerk.' Her follow-up comment — 'So McCain thinks Sarah Palin is wise, but not Sonia?' — underscores the generational shift in values. Hinojosa shares a conversation with a Dominican immigrant cabdriver in Harlem, who sees Sotomayor’s nomination not as pandering, but as overdue political accountability. 'He owes us!' the driver insists. 'Without the Latino vote, you don’t win the presidency.' His demand? Immigration reform — a call for justice for families torn apart by policy. Hinojosa concludes that Sotomayor didn’t just break a barrier — she raised the bar. For her, the challenge now is to fully own the title of 'wise Latina.' And for politicians like McCain? article_content: Washington (CNN) — Republican Dan Sullivan has defeated incumbent Senator Mark Begich in Alaska, CNN projects on Wednesday. 'Today, we begin the process of turning our country around and building a brighter future for our children,' Sullivan said in a statement. An updated vote tally from the Alaska Division of Elections shows Sullivan leading Begich 48.6% to 45.4% as of Wednesday morning. Republicans will now hold at least 53 seats in the U.S. Senate next year, with one final race remaining in Louisiana, set for a December 6 runoff. Begich, a first-term Democrat, faced Sullivan, a first-time candidate originally from Ohio, who sought to nationalize the race by labeling Begich a 'rubber stamp' for President Barack Obama — whose approval ratings remain low in the deeply Republican state. As a senator, Begich voted for Obama’s signature health care law, the Affordable Care Act, which has become a contentious issue in Alaska and other competitive Senate races nationwide. Begich is the fourth Democratic Senate incumbent defeated in the November 4 elections. Throughout the campaign, polling consistently showed Begich trailing Sullivan, prompting Republicans to view Alaska as a prime opportunity to gain a Senate seat and move closer to reclaiming control of the upper chamber. Sullivan campaigned on conservative platforms, including curbing federal spending, restricting abortion access, and expanding infrastructure in rural Alaska. Begich countered by focusing on local priorities: opposing the privatization of Social Security, supporting veterans’ programs, and increasing funding and research for both oil and renewable energy in Alaska’s resource-rich economy. In a campaign advertisement, Begich drew a clear distinction between himself and President Obama, citing disagreements on Arctic drilling and gun rights. 'I am not his candidate,' Begich said, while acknowledging he voted for Obama in both 2008 and 2012. CNN's Robert Yoon and Steve Brusk contributed to this report.

While some may find his actions unconventional, Flores appears to be finding comfort and joy in the simple companionship of his pet — and perhaps, in the quiet freedom of life beyond professional football.

article_content: A Florida cardiologist, Dr. Zannos Grekos, is facing the possible loss of his medical license after a patient died during an unapproved stem cell procedure. The Florida Department of Health issued an emergency suspension on Wednesday, accusing him of breaking state rules banning such treatments and contributing to the death of an elderly patient with severe lung conditions. According to officials, the patient, identified as R.P., suffered cardiac arrest during the procedure. This isn’t Grekos’s first encounter with regulators — back in 2011, a similar emergency ban was enacted after another patient died under his care. In 2009, CNN reported that Grekos claimed to use so-called 'regenocytes,' a term later debunked by leading stem cell experts as scientifically invalid. Though he later admitted the word was merely marketing, the controversy persisted. Grekos, through his publicist, expressed deep sorrow over the patient’s death and denied performing any illegal treatments. He insists he is fully cooperating with ongoing investigations and believes recent media reports have misrepresented the facts. An administrative hearing to formally review the suspension has been delayed until June after Grekos switched legal counsel.

Swiss designers at Micasa Lab have created the Cocoon 1 — a human-sized, transparent bubble designed as a personal retreat for those seeking peace without total disconnection. Made of durable, transparent material, the Cocoon 1 can be placed indoors, outdoors, suspended from ceilings, hung in trees using a custom net, or even floated in water. Its modular design allows users to customize functionality: add sleeping pods, storage units, Wi-Fi, a small kitchen, or even a sink with water drainage. Powered by a portable battery pack, it provides up to 40 hours of lighting or 20 hours of light plus 30 minutes of cooking. With a diameter of 180 cm and weighing 97 kg, the Cocoon 1 is built for stability and comfort. Specially designed ergonomic pillows enhance relaxation, while its playful aesthetic — featuring bright colors and building-block-style modules — evokes the simplicity of children’s toys. Set to launch later in 2012 at a price of $3,000, the Cocoon 1 invites users to carve out moments of calm — whether reading a book in a busy home or nesting among treetops in nature.

article_content: For the first time in her life, three-year-old Kennedy Stevenson from Pennsylvania will sit down to a full Thanksgiving meal — turkey, stuffing, and all — thanks to a groundbreaking liver transplant. Born with an incredibly rare metabolic disorder called S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency, Kennedy’s body could not break down protein, forcing her onto a severely restricted diet of less than 20 grams of plant-based protein per day. The condition, documented in only eight people globally, led to progressive neurological decline. Her journey to recovery began when her mother, Donya McCoy, posted an urgent plea on Facebook seeking a compatible liver donor. Responding to the call was Michael Thompson, a 36-year-old firefighter and former high school classmate of Donya’s. Though not close, Thompson, who shares Kennedy’s blood type, volunteered to donate 25% of his liver. The successful 12-hour surgery, performed two weeks ago, marked what doctors believe is the first such transplant ever conducted for this specific disorder. Now, Kennedy is tasting foods once forbidden: chicken fingers, chocolate milk, and more. Her mother described how Kennedy’s eyes lit up as she sucked on the straw of her chocolate milk, unwilling to let go. Kennedy remains hospitalized at Children’s Hospital of Pittsburgh for recovery, expected to last four months, while her father and stepfather take turns visiting. The diagnosis was nearly missed until Dr. S. Harvey Mudd, an 86-year-old metabolic expert who had retired, recognized the unique brain scan patterns. After Dr. Mudd passed away 11 months later, Dr. Kevin Strauss of the Clinic for Special Children took over her care and recommended the transplant. 'She’s the first in the world to get this done,' Donya said. For Thompson, the decision was simple: 'I was put here on Earth to help people.'

article_content: Former Labour Cabinet Minister James Purnell is at the center of controversy over whether he truly left behind his political past. Appointed to a £295,000-a-year role as BBC Director of Strategy and Digital, Purnell faces skepticism from senior Conservatives due to his decade-long tenure as a Labour MP and former Culture Secretary under Gordon Brown. BBC Director-General Lord Hall insists Purnell has ‘hung up his political boots’ and is now fully impartial. Yet doubts have surfaced after it was revealed that Purnell’s 2013 Who’s Who listing still identifies him as a member of the Stalybridge Labour Club — located in his former parliamentary constituency in Greater Manchester. The BBC initially dismissed the listing as an error, but the club itself confirmed Purnell’s longstanding association. Adding to the confusion, a club stewardess mistook a Mail on Sunday reporter for Purnell and remarked, ‘Sorry, James, a reporter has been on and caught me unawares.’ When pressed, the BBC claimed Purnell left the club in 2010. However, the club’s staff recounted incidents suggesting he visited as recently as last autumn. A Who’s Who representative confirmed that while Purnell updated other personal details since 2010, he never removed his club membership. Tory MP Philip Davies criticized Purnell, stating he ‘has not been totally straight’ about his ties. In response, Purnell acknowledged his Who’s Who profile is outdated and promised to correct it, reiterating he has not been a member since 2010. The BBC further claimed a journalist had impersonated Purnell to contact the club — a claim the club denies. The episode has become a public relations fiasco, highlighting tensions between political legacy and institutional neutrality — especially within the BBC.

BBC yeroo tokko ibsa isaaniis kanaa garaa guddaa jedhan, akkasumas muraataa kanaan isin qabanii dhabamuu qabu. article_content: In late 2012, Nintendo launched the Wii U — a next-generation console designed to redefine home gaming with an innovative tablet-like controller. Unlike previous systems, this new controller featured a full-color touchscreen and dual analog sticks, blending the accessibility of mobile interfaces with the depth expected by core gamers. Rumors suggested the hardware was roughly twice as powerful as the Xbox 360, positioning it as a serious contender in the living room. While Nintendo’s iconic franchises like Super Mario and The Legend of Zelda remained exclusive to its platforms, the company faced mounting pressure from the rise of mobile gaming and cloud-based services. Tech giants like Apple and Google were advancing their own entertainment ecosystems, raising questions about the future of dedicated home consoles. Analysts, including Soichiro Fukuda of Citigroup, warned that traditional gaming hardware might soon become obsolete as consumers increasingly turned to portable devices and streaming solutions. Despite these headwinds, Nintendo bet big on its hybrid approach, hoping the Wii U’s dual-screen experience would carve out a unique niche in an evolving market.

article_content: At just two years apart in age, Australian Open finalists Maria Sharapova and Victoria Azarenka represent two very different chapters in women’s tennis. Sharapova, a former world No. 1 and three-time Grand Slam champion, has spent over a decade in the spotlight — known for her poise, power, and resilience after battling a serious shoulder injury that sidelined her for nearly a year. Now 25, she’s chasing her second Australian Open title, her first final since 2009. Her path to the final included a hard-fought 6-2, 3-6, 6-4 win over Petra Kvitova, a player who stunned her in the 2011 Wimbledon final. In contrast, 22-year-old Victoria Azarenka is experiencing the breakthrough of her career. With no prior Grand Slam final appearance, she’s riding a 11-match winning streak in 2012 and reached her first major final after a dramatic 6-4, 1-6, 6-3 semifinal victory over defending champion Kim Clijsters. Azarenka dug deep after surrendering the second set, breaking Clijsters’ serve in the eighth game of the deciding set to seize momentum and ultimately secure her place in history. Both players are within reach of the world No. 1 ranking — a prize Sharapova once held and Azarenka has never touched. Their head-to-head record stands at 3-3, with each having won their most recent meeting: Sharapova in Rome last year, Azarenka in Miami earlier this year. For Sharapova, a win would symbolize a triumphant return from adversity. For Azarenka, it would mark the arrival of a new era in women’s tennis. 'It means so much to be back in a Grand Slam final,' Sharapova said after her semifinal win. 'I don’t regret anything that’s happened... It’s more about the Grand Slam win than the ranking.' Azarenka echoed similar conviction: 'You can’t just say you believe you’re going to do it — you have to work your way through it.' Sharapova was defeated by Serena Williams in the 2007 Australian Open final — her only previous loss in a Grand Slam final. This time, she aims to turn the script around.

article_content: Last week, British national Chris McManus and Italian citizen Franco Lamolinara were killed by their captors in northern Nigeria during a joint rescue attempt by British and Nigerian forces. The two men, both construction workers, had been held hostage for ten months after being abducted in May 2012 near Birnin-Kebbi. Their kidnappers, believed to be part of a Boko Haram splinter group with suspected links to Al Qaeda, had released videos demanding political concessions — including one in August where McManus, blindfolded and wearing a Manchester United jersey, begged the UK government to act. After months of surveillance and intelligence work, the UK’s Special Boat Service (SBS), working with Nigerian troops, raided a heavily guarded compound in Sokoto, where the hostages were believed to be held. Authorities say they moved in after receiving credible intelligence that the men’s lives were in immediate and escalating peril. Tragically, as forces approached, the captors executed both hostages. British Prime Minister David Cameron personally notified McManus’s family before making a public statement, expressing profound grief and reaffirming the UK’s determination to confront terrorism. He noted this was the second time a UK-hostage rescue had ended in death — the first being the 2009 killing of Scottish aid worker Linda Norgrove in Afghanistan. Italy responded with growing outrage after learning it was not informed of the operation until it was already underway. Former Prime Minister Massimo D’Alema called for a full investigation, asking why Rome was excluded from pre-operation planning. Meanwhile, Nigerian President Goodluck Jonathan confirmed all attackers were captured and none of the 20 British personnel were injured. McManus’s family released a moving statement, thanking everyone who worked to bring him home and extending their sympathies to Lamolinara’s loved ones. They said they had always believed every effort was being made during their agonizing ten months of uncertainty. The men had been working on a bank construction project in Kebbi Province — a volatile region — when armed militants stormed their home. One German colleague survived by climbing over a wall despite being shot.

article_content: Three years after losing her three daughters and both parents in a devastating Christmas morning fire in Stamford, Connecticut, Madonna Badger speaks openly about how the memory of her children has become her lifeline. In a heartfelt conversation with Oprah Winfrey, the 50-year-old advertising professional recalled the chaos of that day — the smoke, the screams, the unbearable silence afterward. Only she and her then-partner, Michael Borcino, escaped the flames. Official reports say the fire began when Borcino placed a bucket of glowing embers from the fireplace into the home’s mud room. But Badger isn’t convinced. She insists she saw sparks fly from an electrical box moments before the inferno took hold. In the darkest hours of her grief, she says her daughters reached out to her — not in dreams, but in the mirror. One day, while weeping uncontrollably in the bathroom, she looked up and saw Sarah, Lily, and Grace standing beside her parents and Borcino, all smiling gently. ‘Sarah spoke to me,’ Badger told Oprah. ‘She said, “Don’t be afraid. Love is everything. Dreams are more real than this life.”’ That moment, she says, changed everything. She called a friend immediately, repeating over and over: ‘It’s real. It’s real. It’s real.’ Though she still wrestles with anger and sorrow, Badger has rebuilt her life. She returned to the advertising agency she co-founded, Badgers & Winters, saying work gave her back her sense of purpose. She also reconnected with William Duke, a friend she’d known since she was 19. They married quietly in Brooklyn this summer. ‘He’s my rock,’ she says. She no longer feels her children when she’s consumed by bitterness — only when she’s at peace. But she hasn’t stopped fighting. Badger sued the city of Stamford after officials demolished her home the very next day, destroying potential evidence. ‘Someone knows what really happened,’ she says. ‘My prayer is that person comes forward.’ Even now, she carries her daughters’ laughter in her heart — the sound of sugar cookies baking, her father coming home as Santa, the warmth of a family Christmas night gone too soon.

article_content: When I asked Abu Omar how he was doing, his answer was grimly familiar: 'Still alive.' It wasn’t just a phrase—it was a survival mantra. We’d last met nearly a year earlier in Damascus, where he and a network of brave civilians had orchestrated a dangerous mission to get journalists into Kafarsouseh, a district under heavy surveillance. To avoid detection, we switched taxis repeatedly under cover of darkness, relying on a simple signal: if my hat was on, we were clear; if it was off, we were followed. For Abu Omar and his team, getting caught meant torture—or worse. Each protest was a fleeting act of courage. Twenty lookouts scanned the alleys for security forces. When the coast was clear, people emerged in pairs, waving flags and chanting, 'O how great is freedom!' Banners were slapped on walls, handwritten slogans fluttered down like confetti—and then, in under fifteen minutes, the warning came. Security forces were closing in. Everyone scattered. These weren’t just rallies; they were acts of defiance that lasted barely longer than a breath. Back then, Abu Omar believed change would come through nonviolence. He thought his neighborhood could become the soul of the revolution. But in late February, soldiers came for him. His father woke him with a whisper: 'They’re here.' He didn’t believe it—until his brother burst in, screaming. What followed was unimaginable: beatings so severe he doesn’t know how he lived. When he was finally released, the world he knew had vanished. The young men he’d marched with were now armed. Some joined the Free Syrian Army to defend protests. Others fought simply to protect their homes and families. The messages I received over Skype turned darker: 'Another martyr today.' The street demonstrations faded as Kafarsouseh became a war zone. Abu Omar himself eventually picked up a weapon—not to fight ideology, but to survive. He filmed from the front lines until a bullet tore into his arm. One of the fighters who saved him died soon after. Abu Omar wanted to say goodbye—but couldn’t reach the body in time. He lost more than friends. He lost a man who’d once been beaten and left for dead in a safehouse, then trained as a medic, helping others—and was later killed. A 27-year-old father of two. And now, even the revolution’s ideals are under threat. Radical Islamist groups are gaining ground. 'We’ve suffered too long,' Abu Omar says. 'No one gets to decide our future for us.' But he knows the road ahead is fractured: democracy is still the dream, but the battlefield has changed.

article_content: As 2015 began, few European leaders felt optimistic. Instead, many worried that the euro and even the European Union itself might start falling apart. At the center of this crisis is Greece — a nation admitted to the eurozone before its economy was ready, now facing another turning point. After failing to elect a president, Greece is headed for a snap election on January 25. Polls show Alexis Tsipras and his left-wing Syriza party are poised to win. Their platform? Rejecting harsh austerity measures imposed by international creditors, reversing wage cuts, and refusing to repay large portions of Greece’s debt. Though Tsipras now says he wants Greece to stay in the euro, experts doubt that’s possible if he follows through on his promises. A Greek exit would mark the first major crack in the euro project. But Greece isn’t alone. In Spain, the anti-austerity party Podemos leads in public opinion. Portugal, still reeling from a €78 billion bailout, is rocked by corruption scandals involving top officials. Even in Italy, three of the four largest parties — Forza Italia, the Northern League, and the Five Star Movement — are openly questioning their commitment to the EU. Perhaps the greatest threat lies in the United Kingdom. Though it never adopted the euro, the UK’s May 2015 general election could reshape the entire bloc. The euroskeptic UK Independence Party (UKIP) has been steadily eroding support from both the Conservatives and Labour. With the Liberal Democrats weakened and the Scottish National Party gaining ground, no party seems likely to win outright. If Prime Minister David Cameron leads a coalition, he’ll be forced to honor his promise of an EU referendum by 2017. To appease UKIP, he’s pushed for stricter limits on EU migrants and their access to welfare — positions that could clash with EU principles. If Brussels refuses to compromise on free movement, Cameron’s promises may collapse, pushing more Britons to vote 'Out.' article_content: Belfast, Northern Ireland (CNN) — Under a gray, overcast sky, more than 1,000 protesters gathered Saturday in Belfast, carrying large Union flags, some draped over their shoulders. The silent demonstration outside City Hall began peacefully, the quiet broken only by the hum of helicopters circling overhead conducting surveillance. Hours later, clashes erupted between Protestant demonstrators and police. As the march passed through a predominantly Catholic neighborhood, bottles were thrown between groups. Police, supported by dozens of armored vehicles, were heavily present. The rally, followed by a march to East Belfast, is the latest in a wave of protests triggered by Belfast City Council’s December 3 decision to limit the flying of the Union flag to 18 days per year — ending a century-long tradition of displaying it daily over City Hall. Protests also occurred across Northern Ireland on Friday night. While most remained peaceful, disturbances broke out in several areas. The most serious incident occurred on O’Neill’s Road in Newtownabbey, where approximately 100 Protestant demonstrators — many teenagers — hurled concrete blocks, paving slabs, bricks, wooden planks, gasoline bombs, and Molotov cocktails at around 30 armored police vehicles and up to 100 officers in riot gear. Four officers were injured, one requiring hospitalization; two individuals were arrested. Amid rain and temperatures just above freezing, police deployed two water cannons, using one to disperse rioters. Temperatures are expected to drop further Saturday as protesters continue their march to East Belfast, a recent hotspot for unrest. The city had endured five consecutive nights of rioting earlier in the week. Leaders of Northern Ireland’s two main unionist parties met Thursday to address community concerns. The Union flag was raised Wednesday — for the first time since the vote — to mark the birthday of Prince William’s wife, Catherine, and was lowered at day’s end. Authorities accuse loyalist extremists of exploiting the flag policy change to incite violence. The Union flag has long symbolized identity and division: for Protestant loyalists, it represents ties to Britain; for Catholic nationalists, it signifies exclusion from an Irish identity. Northern Ireland’s partition in 1921 followed Ireland’s independence, with six of Ulster’s nine counties choosing to remain in the UK. The conflict known as 'The Troubles' — spanning three decades and claiming over 3,000 lives — ended with the 1998 Good Friday Agreement. Under the accord, paramilitary groups disarmed, and Sinn Féin joined a power-sharing government with pro-British parties. Yet deep mistrust persists. The term 'Union Jack' is often used interchangeably with 'Union Flag.' While some argue 'Jack' applies only when flown on naval vessels, the UK Flag Institute states this distinction is relatively modern and not widely observed.

article_content: In the quiet town of Dawsonville, Georgia, something extraordinary is happening — legal moonshine is being distilled right inside the city hall building. No longer hidden in backwoods stills, this historic spirit is now produced under the same roof as town officials, marking what experts say is the first such operation of its kind in the United States. Led by local entrepreneurs like Cheryl 'Happy' Wood and veteran distillers Dwight Bearden and Bob Suchke, the Dawsonville Moonshine Distillery isn’t just making liquor — it’s reviving a legacy. For generations, families here made moonshine not for profit alone, but as survival: a cough remedy for sick children, extra cash during hard winters, and even the fuel behind the high-speed car chases that gave birth to NASCAR. The distillery’s space, leased from the city, sits beside the Georgia Racing Hall of Fame Museum, tying past to present. Corn from nearby farms, apples from Ellijay, and copper stills passed down through families are all part of the process. No added sugars. No shortcuts. 'This ain't sugar liquor,' Wood insists. 'This is the real deal.' City leaders see it as more than nostalgia. Mayor W. James Grogan says the project strengthens Dawsonville’s identity and draws tourism. State law doesn’t yet allow sales on-site, but visitors can sample the spirit, and lawmakers are considering bills to let tourists buy a single bottle as a keepsake. Outside, old Ford coupes sit rusting near the building — relics of Thunder Road, where bootleggers once raced toward Atlanta, chased by federal agents. Today, those same roads slow for school zones. But inside city hall, the hum of the still echoes louder than ever — a living tribute to resilience, heritage, and the quiet revolution of local craftsmanship.

article_content: National Geographic has unveiled its 2014 Annual Photo Contest, showcasing a stunning selection of entries from photographers around the world. The submissions—spanning animals, people, and landscapes—reflect the organization’s enduring commitment to photographic excellence. Last year, the contest received more than 7,000 entries from over 150 countries, drawing both professional photographers and passionate amateurs. This year’s competition features three categories: People, Places, and Nature. Standout images include playful polar bear cubs on an ice floe in Svalbard, Norway; a flock of galahs soaring near a water source in Australia’s Strezlecki Desert; a Mediterranean mantis mid-wing-spread in Cyprus; and a serene close-up of a manatee at Point Defiance Zoo in Washington state. Other breathtaking shots capture lupine fields glowing under California’s sky, the soft pink hues of a sunset reflecting in Iceland’s Jökulsárlón Glacier Lagoon, and Mexican women in Oaxaca adorned with intricate face paint for Día de los Muertos. The Grand Prize winner will receive $10,000 and an all-expenses-paid trip to National Geographic’s headquarters in Washington, D.C., to attend the January 2015 Photography Seminar. First-place winners in each category will earn $2,500 and have their photos published in National Geographic magazine. Entries close on October 31, 2014. Photographers shared heartfelt stories behind their work: Colin Mackenzie described watching the polar bear cubs with delight; Hasan Ba Iar marveled at how sunlight transformed the mantis’s wings; Misty Gage was moved by the manatee’s curious gaze; Francesco Riccardo Iacomino called his Iceland image a 'dreamscape' born from patience and fading light; Montse Grillo saw divine majesty in a sea turtle emerging from the waves; Douglas Croft found unexpected beauty above the fog in Big Sur; Daniel Kudish honored the vibrant celebration of life in Oaxaca; Thomas Dorleans likened the Taj Mahal’s morning mist to a hallucination; and Aaron Feinberg celebrated the intricate textures of an agave plant in San Francisco.

article_content: A 2011 study by researchers at University College London found that non-European migrants living in the UK between 1995 and 2011 cost public finances approximately £118.1 billion over that period. During these 17 years, these migrants consistently received more in public services and benefits than they paid in taxes. In contrast, migrants from the European Economic Area (EEA) — including those from Western and Eastern Europe — contributed a net total of £4.425 billion over the same timeframe. While they were net recipients in seven of the 17 years, they were net contributors in the remaining ten. The report noted that EEA migrants arriving after 2000 made a larger net contribution of £20 billion, largely driven by high-earning professionals from countries like Germany and France (£15 billion), followed by Eastern European workers (£5 billion). However, the study also revealed that native-born Britons themselves were net recipients of public funds in 12 of the 17 years — a result of rising unemployment, expanded welfare spending during the 2008 financial crisis, and lower tax contributions relative to benefit usage. The total fiscal imbalance across the entire population — including both migrants and natives — amounted to over £541 billion during this period, reflecting deep structural deficits in public finances. Critics argue the report presents an incomplete picture. They point out that it measures only direct fiscal flows, ignoring long-term societal investments such as education, housing, and labor market integration. Some also question whether the study accounts for the social costs of rapid population growth — such as pressure on schools, NHS capacity, and community cohesion. Sir Andrew Green of MigrationWatch stated the findings confirm that immigration has imposed substantial costs over the past two decades. Meanwhile, David Green of Civitas criticized the authors for 'shallow calculations,' noting that the arrival of educated migrants coincided with a decline in apprenticeships for British youth — a significant social trade-off. The study concludes in 2011, just as the UK economy began recovering — leaving out critical developments in migration policy and economic conditions since then.

article_content: On Tuesday, Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami for the second straight day to receive updates on the rescue mission for 41 workers trapped inside the Silkyara tunnel in Uttarkashi — now in its tenth day. Dhami shared via social media that all workers remain safe and that the Prime Minister reiterated the rescue operation as the nation’s top priority. This marks the fourth time Modi has personally checked in with Dhami since the tunnel collapsed on November 12 after a landslide. Dhami reported that rescuers had successfully installed a 6-inch pipeline through the debris, allowing for the delivery of increased quantities of food and critical supplies. He also informed the Prime Minister that an endoscopic camera, flown in from Delhi late Monday, had captured the first-ever video of the workers. In the footage, the men — wearing yellow and white helmets — were seen eating meals passed through the pipeline and calmly conversing. Before this, rescuers relied on a smaller 4-inch tube to supply oxygen, medicine, and dried fruits. Located roughly 30 kilometers from Uttarkashi town and a seven-hour drive from Dehradun, the Silkyara tunnel is part of the central government’s ambitious Char Dham all-weather road project designed to ensure year-round access to sacred pilgrimage sites. Rescue teams continue working nonstop, determined to bring every worker home safely.

article_content: Passengers aboard the South Korean ferry Sewol sent desperate, heartfelt messages to their families moments before the vessel sank. As the boat listed violently, children and adults alike reached for their phones in a final attempt to connect with loved ones. Twenty-four people, including five students and two teachers from Danwon High School, have been confirmed dead. Another 272 remain unaccounted for, feared trapped inside the submerged hull. One student sent a text message to his mother: 'No phone connection, so no internet — just sending a text. There are few people on the ship. It’s completely dark. Women are screaming, but we’re not dead yet — please pass this along.' Another passenger, addressing members of his school theater group, wrote: 'If I’ve wronged any of you, forgive me. I love you guys.' A third student told his mother, 'I’m sending this now because I’m afraid I won’t get another chance to say it — I love you.' His mother replied, 'Why…? I was wondering why you weren’t checking Messenger…' Then added, 'Me too, son. I love you.' He was later rescued and reunited with his family. Family members on shore sent messages back, urging those trapped to stay calm. One brother told his sibling: 'Keep calm. Don’t panic. Take your time. Stay sharp. Do what they say. When you get signal, contact me again — your brother.' However, authorities warn that hoax messages claiming to be from passengers are spreading. The ferry’s captain, 69-year-old Lee Joon-seok, is under investigation for allegedly abandoning ship while instructing passengers to remain in place. Reports indicate only one of the 46 lifeboats was deployed as the vessel capsized. Rescuers, including divers and submersibles, are hammering on the upturned hull and reportedly pumping oxygen into the submerged sections, though the coast guard has not officially confirmed these efforts. The Sewol capsized on Wednesday, April 16, 2014, during a routine trip from Incheon to Jeju Island. Hundreds of grieving relatives gathered on nearby Jindo Island, waiting for news. Some, like parent Park Yung-suk, watched as the body of her daughter’s teacher was brought ashore. 'If I could learn to dive,' she said, 'I’d jump in and find my daughter.' South Korean Prime Minister Chung Hong-won faced public fury when a distraught family member threw a water bottle at him. Parents accused officials of slow response and withholding information. 'I’m furious with the government,' said Kwak Hyun-ok, whose daughter was among the students on board. This is the deadliest maritime disaster in South Korea since 1993, when 292 people died in the Donghae ferry accident.

article_content: In early January 2013, Brighton and Hove City Council began urgent repairs on Preston Park’s aging pond — the first major overhaul in twenty years. To safely relocate the pond’s estimated 1,000 resident fish — including goldfish, perch, and coy carp — officials placed them in large, insulated rubbish skips on-site, hoping to prevent vandalism and keep them secure during construction. But as freezing temperatures set in, the water in the skips couldn’t be refreshed regularly without creating icy hazards on nearby footpaths and bike lanes. Without proper aeration, oxygen levels dropped, leading to the deaths of around 40 fish. A concerned passerby noticed dead fish floating in the skips and alerted the RSPCA. The animal welfare group immediately contacted the council, warning that the skips were unsuitable for long-term fish housing. They helped arrange the safe transfer of the surviving fish to a nearby facility with properly maintained ponds. While the RSPCA stated there wasn’t enough evidence to pursue legal action, they publicly criticized the council’s planning and emphasized the need for better contingency measures in extreme weather. Geoff Raw, the council’s Strategic Director, expressed deep sorrow over the loss, calling the incident ‘very regrettable.’ He explained that staff, many of whom are passionate conservationists, were devastated and never intended harm. The council has since committed to working closely with the RSPCA to improve future wildlife handling protocols.

article_content: On Friday morning, a woman vandalized the Brooklyn Wall of Remembrance at MCU Park in Coney Island, smearing white paint over the image of Officer Moira Smith—the only female NYPD officer killed during the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks. The incident occurred between 2:38 a.m. and 2:55 a.m., when the memorial was unattended. According to police, the suspect, described as a white woman in her late 40s to early 50s, used her paint-covered hands to deface Smith’s engraved image and surrounding area. Surveillance footage shows her wearing a fluorescent green top and flowing skirt, calmly walking past security cameras while handling something in her hands. In addition to damaging Smith’s memorial, the vandal left behind paint, liquor bottles, and debris. Eyewitnesses reported that the image of Detective Joseph Vigiano was also defaced, though the most extensive damage was concentrated on Smith’s panel. Officer Smith, 38, was celebrated for her bravery on 9/11. She helped evacuate civilians—including broker Edward Nicholls—from the South Tower of the World Trade Center before returning to assist others. She was killed when the tower collapsed. The Brooklyn Wall of Remembrance, New York City’s first 9/11 memorial honoring first responders, displays engraved portraits of 346 FDNY firefighters, 37 Port Authority officers, 23 NYPD officers, three New York State officers, one fire patrol officer, and a rescue dog. Smith’s daughter, Patricia, was only two years old when her mother died. Her husband, James Smith, a retired NYPD officer, was unaware of the vandalism until notified by authorities. 'It’s kind of strange,' he told The New York Daily News. Councilman Mark Treyger called the act 'despicable' and publicly thanked the NYPD for its rapid response. He shared photos of the damage on social media, urging accountability. The NYPD is now asking the public for help identifying the suspect. Tips can be submitted anonymously via the Crime Stoppers hotline at 800-577-TIPS, online at nypdcrimestoppers.com, or by texting 'CRIMES' to 274637 and entering code TIP577.

article_content: By Chris Parsons. Last updated at 10:28 AM on 7th December 2011. A festive ice rink erected in Evesham’s town center has been labeled a 'diabolical mess' after contractors installed it on a sloped surface. Hundreds of parents and children were left disappointed by the poorly constructed winter attraction in Evesham’s Market Square, where uneven flooring resembled a cobbled street. Due to health and safety concerns, the hazardous rink was dismantled less than three weeks before Christmas. Inspectors determined last Friday that the rink was unsafe. Despite attempts by contractors to fix the issues, the attraction was closed over the weekend. The rink’s foundation was not level, and dozens of panels were misaligned, creating tripping hazards along the edges and center. Father-of-two Daniel Lewis, 45, said: 'The ice rink looked downright hazardous. It sat on a steep slope in places, and the panels stuck up everywhere—like a cobbled street. My kids were gutted. They were inconsolable when I told them they couldn’t skate.' Evesham town clerk Frank Green noted: 'We’ve worked with this company for two years without incident, but this year’s rink was different. The floor panels were uneven and dangerous. The sides were unsuitable too.' After Friday’s inspection, the contractor was asked to correct the issues. Further checks on Saturday confirmed unresolved safety risks. Evesham Town Council ordered the 50ft by 50ft rink from Skate Spectacular. Mayor Cllr Jim Bulman called it 'a diabolical mess' and said it ruined the town’s holiday plans. Ronald Bishton, owner of Worcestershire-based Skate Spectacular, admitted the error: 'It’s just gone pear-shaped. I wasn’t there, so I don’t know what went wrong. I’m gutted. I’ve offered to provide another rink at a reduced rate next year.'

article_content: The UK edition of Elle has come under fire for its latest cover, which features Pharrell Williams wearing a feathered headdress. Thousands of social media users labeled the image as 'disrespectful' and 'racist,' pointing out that the traditional feather headdress is a sacred symbol in many Native American cultures. Within hours of the July issue’s release, users flooded both Pharrell’s and Elle UK’s Facebook pages with criticism, using the hashtag #NotHappy—a play on his hit song 'Happy.' One user wrote: 'Bad move, Elle… very disrespectful. He has no business wearing that.' Another stated: 'Please stop your stylists from exploiting Native culture in photo shoots. You should know better.' A third added: 'Are you kidding me? This is the most disturbing, overtly racist co-optation of a cultural object.' Feathered headdresses, or war bonnets, were historically worn by Native American chiefs and warriors who earned each feather through acts of bravery or service. According to Wikipedia, their primary purpose is spiritual protection. Eagle feathers, especially, were highly revered, and the most honored warriors often hunted their own eagles. Though warfare is no longer part of contemporary Native life, the headdress remains a sacred item, used in ceremonies and passed down through generations. Others used the moment to educate: Ruth Rose explained, 'The headdress is sacred—it was worn by those chosen and revered to lead the people. It is not a fashion accessory.' Eric Garcia compared its misuse to wearing the Medal of Honor, America’s highest military decoration: 'Would you appreciate it if a foreign nation photographed people wearing the Medal of Honor?' Yesterday, Pharrell issued an apology through a representative to the New York Daily News: 'I respect and honor every race, background, and culture. I am genuinely sorry.' This image is a limited-edition cover released alongside one featuring Keira Knightley. Originally, the Elle UK website described the shoot as: 'We persuaded Elle Style Award winner Pharrell to trade his Vivienne Westwood mountie hat for a Native American feather headdress in his best-ever shoot.' These words have since been removed. Pharrell, pictured on The Today Show, appeared cheerful during a performance at Rockefeller Plaza, but the controversy overshadowed the moment. Similar controversies have occurred before: Chanel’s December 2023 fashion show in Dallas, which featured models in feather headdresses, was widely condemned as an 'offensive mockery' by Native American activists. In recent years, retailers including Victoria’s Secret, Urban Outfitters, and H&M, as well as the band No Doubt, have all apologized for using Native American attire as fashion statements.

article_content: Exeter Chiefs delivered a commanding performance at Sandy Park, bouncing back from their narrow loss to Newcastle with a decisive 44-24 win over London Irish. Fly-half Gareth Steenson was the heartbeat of the attack, kicking 19 points and playing a direct role in nearly every try. The home side exploded out of the gates, scoring three tries in the first half through Carl Rimmer, Henry Slade, and Damian Welch—each converted by Steenson—and adding three penalties to build a commanding 30-3 halftime lead. London Irish managed only a single penalty from Shane Geraghty during that stretch. After the break, Exeter didn’t slow down. Seventeen minutes into the second half, Welch crossed again for his second try, followed moments later by Don Armand’s blistering 25-meter sprint to seal the bonus point. Steenson converted both, keeping his perfect kicking record intact. Exeter’s attacking fluidity was on full display: Jack Nowell drew defenders before slipping a pass to Welch, and later, a clever offload from Nowell set Armand free for the final try. London Irish, though outclassed for most of the game, refused to quit. With David Paice sent to the sin bin for illegally blocking a quick tap penalty, the visitors capitalized on their numerical advantage. Replacement flanker Blair Cowan scored twice, and full-back Andrew Fenby added a third late try—all converted by Geraghty—but it was too little, too late. The final whistle confirmed Exeter’s return to form and Irish’s first away defeat of the season. Exeter made four changes to their starting XV, bringing back Mitch Lees and Rimmer in the forwards, while Sam Hill and Jack Nowell returned in the backs. London Irish also rotated their squad, with Tom Guest, Scott Steele, Eamonn Sheridan, and Topsy Ojo coming in. A key moment came early when Exeter missed a golden 10-meter penalty chance after a rushed tap-and-go, but Steenson calmly slotted the next opportunity from five meters out to open the scoring. Referee Ian Tempest, officiating his first Aviva Premiership match, relied on TMO David Grashoff to confirm Rimmer’s opening try, setting the tone for a tightly monitored contest.

article_content: Late one night in Brunswick, a harmless moment turned violent. Two women were dancing at the Penny Black pub on Sydney Road when a man approached them and attempted to forcibly press their heads together to make them kiss. Their boyfriends stepped in, leading to a heated exchange that ended with the aggressor being removed by security. But the night wasn’t over. Around 1:20 a.m., as the two men left the venue, they were ambushed by a group of seven men — including the one who’d been ejected. Without warning, they were punched, beaten, and kicked in the head until they lost consciousness. Emergency crews rushed the pair — 21-year-old and 23-year-old men from Reservoir — to hospital, where they were treated for facial fractures, a concussion, and broken teeth. Police released chilling footage showing the brutal attack in a dark alley, sparking widespread condemnation. Detective Senior Constable Bryan Strangman called the assault 'very unexpected, very cowardly.' Authorities are now hunting the suspects, described as men in their 20s with Middle Eastern features, and are urging witnesses to contact Crime Stoppers with any information.

article_content: A 21-month-old toddler, Poppy Boothroyd, died after being struck by a reversing Ford Transit van in a residential cul-de-sac in Huddersfield. She was under the care of a family friend at the time. Poppy had wandered into the road, and the driver failed to see her as he reversed. Neighbors, alerted by screams, rushed outside to help. One woman, Lynn Marie Richardson, performed CPR in a desperate attempt to save the child. Despite emergency responders arriving and administering oxygen, Poppy was pronounced dead upon arrival at the hospital. Her parents, Melissa McKay and Jordan Boothroyd, described her in a statement as 'an amazing little girl' and 'our perfect little angel.' The incident occurred at 2:24 p.m. on Wednesday in St James Way, Rawthorpe, as Jessica McDonagh, the family friend, was taking Poppy to a local shop. Lynn Richardson, who had just seen the van driver leave her home moments earlier, recalled the chaos: 'I saw the baby on the floor... I did what had to be done.' The driver, a BT contractor, was visibly shaken and immediately aware of what had happened. Neighbors expressed sympathy for him as well. Flowers, teddy bears, and messages of condolence have been left at the scene by grieving friends and residents. West Yorkshire Police are continuing their investigation. BT confirmed the driver was a contractor working on its behalf.

article_content: At the Batam Center International Ferry Terminal on Indonesia’s Batam Island, immigration officials have enforced a strict silent-zone policy: speaking—or even using a mobile phone—in the immigration queue may result in immediate deportation. According to reports from The Straits Times, even whispers or casual conversation can lead to travelers being turned away and sent back on the next ferry to Singapore or Malaysia. A sign featuring a raised finger over closed lips now greets visitors, signaling the zero-tolerance rule implemented this month. One traveler, Guo Kai, told The Straits Times he and a friend were deported after briefly chatting while waiting in line. 'I was there for a holiday—why couldn’t I open my mouth? I was just chit-chatting with my friend,' he said, adding that he had no idea the penalty was so severe. About 50 Singaporean visitors are reportedly turned back each week, according to The Real Singapore. The one-hour ferry ride from Singapore to Batam, costing roughly £24, is a popular choice for weekend getaways. Irwanto Suhaili, chief of the Batam Center Immigration Office, defended the policy, stating that silence is essential for officers to clearly call passengers’ names and maintain orderly processing. While similar rules exist at the Sekupang Ferry Terminal on Batam, they are not consistently enforced.

article_content: At 82, Peter Bradley from Sheffield has spent over half a century behind the wheel of Porsches — and somehow, not once has he gotten a speeding ticket. Despite owning more than 20 of them since his first purchase in 1957 and logging a staggering million miles, his driving record remains spotless. He credits his flawless streak not to luck, but to a profound respect for the machines he drives. Bradley, who still helps run his family’s refrigeration business, says driving a Porsche isn’t about showing off — it’s about savoring the ride. 'It’s like riding a champion racehorse,' he explains. 'You don’t push it to prove something; you let it carry you with grace.' His love affair began with a pale blue 356 model, bought straight from the Porsche factory in Germany for £1,200. He drove it across Europe, covering 6,000 miles just to get home, stopping in Paris for its first service. Before Porsches, he owned VW Beetles, but always dreamed of something more refined — something that finished races, not just led them. He remembers watching Porsches dominate endurance events, not because they were the fastest, but because they never broke down. That reliability became his standard. Over the decades, he’s owned everything from a 911T in the '60s to a 944 in '89 and a 997S, which he returned after six months because it felt 'too quick' for his taste. Though he’s been pulled over once — decades ago, before penalty points existed — he’s never accumulated a single traffic violation. 'I’ve seen so many Porsches built, I could probably put one together blindfolded,' he laughs. He keeps each car for a couple of years, sometimes owning multiple at once, and admits he’s lost count of how much he’s spent. But for him? Every pound has been worth it.

article_content: Queens, New York (CNN) — For Victor Guevares, winning a bid at a chaotic foreclosure auction two months ago was just the beginning of his journey to homeownership. After navigating multiple hurdles, he and his family have now moved into a two-story, three-bedroom home in Queens. Guevares, second from right, purchased the property at a USHomeAuction.com foreclosure sale. Though the auction seemed straightforward, he warns others: 'If you’re going to an auction, do your research.' CNN first met the Guevares family in March, when he secured a home once valued at $527,000 for just $230,000. At the time, banks were rapidly offloading foreclosed homes, many selling at 50% to 60% below peak prices. Foreclosure activity surged in early 2009. According to RealtyTrac, first-quarter filings — including defaults, auction notices, and repossessions — hit a record 803,489, a 24% increase from the prior year. March alone saw 341,180 filings, up 17% from February and 46% from March 2008. On March 8, Guevares sat nervously as bids climbed past $100,000, then $200,000. When the hammer fell, he won with a $230,000 bid. But the real costs began immediately: $7,000 in auction fees and a mandatory $5,000 bidder deposit. Complicating matters further, title records indicated a potential code violation, delaying his mortgage approval. After an inspection cleared the issue, closing day arrived — and with it, the deed to his first home. Still, the work wasn’t done. The house had been split into two apartments. To make it livable for his wife and two children, Guevares demolished a wall, rebuilt the staircase, installed new flooring, repainted, and added a sunroom. Total investment: roughly $280,000 — about $20,000 under the home’s estimated market value. After 12 years of renting, Guevares says the gamble paid off: 'My mortgage is $300 less than what I paid in rent.' Though the backyard remains cluttered with debris, the family moved in last week. His 8-year-old son, Devin, beams in his bright green room, where he can watch the neighbor’s yard — and their dog, Rocky, whose name matches their own pet. 'I can just scream now,' Devin says — a small joy made possible by finally having a home of his own.

Experts advise minimizing risk by opting for ammonia-free formulas, waiting until after the first trimester, avoiding direct scalp contact, wearing masks, and rinsing thoroughly. 'Natural hair is darker at the roots anyway — if you can wear it with confidence, you absolutely should.' The couple announced their pregnancy in October 2014, with most outlets estimating a spring 2015 due date. While they’ve kept details private, Lively’s quiet confidence in embracing her natural look may be inspiring a new wave of pregnancy beauty norms — one where roots aren’t hidden, but celebrated.

article_content: Fernandinho and Yaya Touré were sent off as Manchester City suffered a damaging 2-1 defeat to CSKA Moscow in the Champions League. Both players were dismissed in the second half as City struggled to recover in a Group E match they desperately needed to win to revive their campaign. Seydou Doumbia was once again City’s nemesis, scoring both goals for CSKA — replicating his influential performance in last month’s 2-2 draw in Moscow. Sportsmail’s Joe Bernstein reported from the Etihad Stadium, highlighting several key moments. A Manchester City fan’s banner criticizing UEFA’s handling of CSKA Moscow fans was removed by stewards. Despite a ban, some CSKA supporters gained entry to the stadium and were escorted out by police. Protests erupted among City fans: Yaya Touré publicly condemned racism on Twitter, and supporters booed the Champions League anthem after being denied the chance to travel to Moscow two weeks earlier. CSKA Moscow is required to play home matches behind closed doors due to racist incidents, but City fans were furious when Russian supporters slipped into the Etihad during the previous draw. Fireworks lit up the night sky above the Etihad to mark Bonfire Night, creating a smoky, chilly atmosphere reminiscent of Dickensian London. Yet Seydou Doumbia thrived in the conditions — born in Abidjan, Ivory Coast, where November temperatures average 30°C, he was clearly too hot for City’s defense. Manchester City’s two-for-one ticket initiative helped avoid a repeat of the embarrassing 10,000-empty-seat scenario seen against Roma, but hundreds remained outside at kickoff, and the crowd’s energy remained flat, especially in the first half, where the only significant noise came after Touré’s equalizer — followed by jeers at the halftime whistle. Manager Manuel Pellegrini, perhaps taking a cue from West Ham boss Sam Allardyce, who advised him to be more tactically flexible in Europe, replaced Stevan Jovetic and Jesus Navas at halftime with Fernandinho and Samir Nasri to add midfield steel. It made little difference. Fernandinho lasted only 25 minutes as a substitute before receiving a second yellow card and being sent off.

article_content: A 71-year-old woman in Palm Desert, California, survived a terrifying encounter with a massive swarm of Africanized honey bees—estimated at 75,000 to 80,000—after the colony was disturbed in an underground Verizon vault on Lucerne Drive. The incident occurred Thursday afternoon when the woman, visiting family from out of state, was walking from her car around 4:40 p.m. Unable to escape quickly, she was overwhelmed by the aggressive insects. Family members reacted swiftly, covering her with a blanket and rushing her indoors. According to Lance Davis, owner of Killer Bee Custom Bee Removal, the sheer density of bees made her nearly invisible. 'They’re quick to anger and won’t stop until they feel the threat is gone,' he said. Five firefighters who responded to the scene were also stung and briefly hospitalized, though all have since returned to duty. Davis, who safely removed the bees using smoke to disrupt their pheromone signals and a vacuum to collect them, noted the bees likely chose the vault because it offered shelter and cool temperatures—common traits that attract swarms to attics and wall cavities. He transported the live bees to his apiary in Thermal and later donated them to local farmers for pollination. Authorities and experts alike stress: never attempt to remove or kill bees yourself. Always contact a licensed professional.
